articles.title: Military government in Guinea-Bissau seeks to reshape political system with referendum
articles.author: Nicholas Mwangi
articles.content: Guinea-Bissau is set to vote on a new constitution on Sunday, August 30, in a referendum that could alter the country’s political system and strengthen the powers of the presidency. The referendum comes nine months after the military seized control. The crisis traces back to November 23, 2025, when Guinea-Bissau held presidential and parliamentary elections. Both incumbent President Umaro Sissoco Embaló and opposition candidate Fernando Dias da Costa claimed victory. Before the electoral commission could release provisional results, the military intervened on November 26, one day ahead of the announcement suspending the vote count and arresting opposition figures including PAIGC leader Domingos Simões Pereira and PRS’s Francisco da Costa. General Horta N’Tam was installed as transitional president. What the new constitution would change The draft marks a major rebalancing of power. Currently, the parliamentary majority largely determines the government. Under the proposed system, the president would gain authority to appoint and dismiss the prime minister and ministers, chair the Council of Ministers, restructure ministries, and dissolve Parliament under certain conditions, including once per term without needing Council of State approval. The draft also shrinks Parliament from 102 to 61 seats and cuts electoral constituencies from 29 to 12, changes analysts warn could disadvantage locally-rooted parties and consolidate power among larger blocs. Opposition says referendum risks consolidating military-backed rule Zizwe Tchiguka of the African Party for the Independence of Guinea-Bissau and Cape Verde (PAIGC), speaking about the political crisis and the proposed constitutional changes to BreakThrough News, described the November 2025 military intervention as a “fake coup” designed to prevent the opposition from taking power. The coup is not seen in the same breath as the coups in the AES fight for sovereignty rather than its a safeguarding of the ruling class interests. “The day before the election results were supposed to be announced last November 26, 2025,” Tchiguka said, “the previous illegal president, Umar Sissoko Mbalo, staged a fake coup d’etat.” He questioned why the former president was able to leave the country while opposition figures were arrested. “How could you have a coup d’etat but you could be interviewed by the press and then you could go and get on a plane and leave the country?” he asked. “But the opposition candidates are arrested at the same time.” According to Tchiguka, the arrests included PAIGC leader Domingos Simões Pereira and Francisco da Costa of the Social Renewal Party (PRS), which had participated in the opposition coalition. Domingos Simões Pereira of the PAIGC. Photo: Communist Party of Portugal His concern is that the proposed constitution could fundamentally alter the balance between the presidency, the prime minister and Parliament. “The military regime is trying to change the constitution so that the person who is elected as the President can make the prime minister powerless, null and void,” Tchiguka said, describing this as one of the key features of the proposed constitutional arrangement. He argued that the changes could be used to ensure that an administration acceptable to the military establishment retains effective control even if opposition forces perform strongly in the elections. “So that if they could manipulate the election, they could prevent the opposition party, which is led by Domingos Simões Pereira, from having any power,” he said. Tchiguka further argued that control over Parliament is particularly important because of Simões Pereira’s position within the legislative system. “If you know he’s the president of the parliament, he’s the president of the Legislative Assembly, he would be the second most powerful person in the government,” he said. “What they’re trying to do is to position the person who they can have put in power by a bogus election,” he added, “to make it so that he will be powerless to do anything.” Tchiguka also challenges the legality and timing of the referendum, arguing that constitutional changes should not be undertaken so close to an election. “This idea of having a referendum on the constitution is illegal because ECOWAS, Economic Community of West African States, has a law that you cannot change the constitution no earlier than six months prior to the election date,” he said. He similarly says that Guinea-Bissau’s own legal framework prevents constitutional amendments or a referendum within six months of an election. “This is the scenario that we’re faced with,” he said, “to try to change the constitution this coming Sunday, August the 30th, and to try to set up another election on December the 6th.” Opposition calls for restoration of constitutional order The opposition and allies internationally have called for the restoration of constitutional institutions, the release of political prisoners, the reopening of party headquarters that were shut, and guarantees for political activity. The International Network in Solidarity with Guinea-Bissau is also calling for soldiers to return to the barracks and for conditions that allow political activists to participate freely in the electoral process. Tchiguka said opposition forces are urging citizens not to participate in what they regard as an illegitimate electoral process. “We’re telling the masses of people in Guinea-Bissau, do not go out. Don’t participate in this false election process,” he said. But he also described a second strategy should the referendum and subsequent elections proceed. “Even if they manage to get the people to come out and vote, our next plan is to put pressure on the government, that is the illegal government,” he said. The objective, he explained, would be to ensure that the elected National Assembly retains its constitutional role. “What we’re saying is that even if they manage to pass this bogus constitution, you still have this legislative assembly that should be in place,” Tchiguka said. He pointed to the continued occupation of opposition party headquarters and restrictions on the National Assembly as evidence, in his view, that constitutional institutions have yet to be fully restored. “They presently occupy the headquarters of the PAIGC,” he said, “and they presently have the People’s National Assembly locked out of the assembly building.” The vote unfolds with unresolved questions over the transitional government’s legitimacy, the uncertified November 2025 results, and the fairness of December’s elections. Tchiguka also adds that Embaló remains politically active and could benefit from a path back to power, part of the opposition’s broader reading of the crisis. He concludes that the situation represents “a real desperate situation for the illegal military regime to try to stay in power.”

articles.title: Health activists in India demand affordable breast cancer treatments
articles.author: Ana Vračar
articles.content: Health activists and public health experts in India are pushing for affordable breast cancer treatments as the Kerala High Court continues to hear a case originally filed in 2022. The case and the surrounding advocacy concern access to the medications ribociclib and abemaciclib – both of which have demonstrated significant benefits for patients with early-stage breast cancer but remain prohibitively expensive for a large part of the population. Breast cancer represents a true public health crisis in India, noted the Working Group on Access to Medicines and Treatment. In 2024 , of the 780,000 new cancer cases among women, breast cancer accounted for 237,000 diagnoses. India also has a notable survival gap compared to other countries: five-year survival stands at 65.7%, compared to 87.3% in high-income countries. “The price of the treatment is one of the biggest barriers,” the Working Group noted. “Ribociclib costs around 75,000 rupees (approximately USD 786) a month. A three-year course can therefore cost close to 27 lakh rupees (approximately USD 28,300). Abemaciclib costs roughly 48,000–95,000 rupees (approximately USD 500-995) a month. Such prices put these medicines beyond the reach of most families.” Members of the working group stress that the high cost stems from the treatments’ market positioning. “Ribociclib and abemaciclib remain available mainly as expensive branded medicines and are not routinely available through government support programs,” they point out, with a significant impact on rural and poor patients. “Nearly 100,000 women are dying of breast cancer every year. If that is not a public health emergency, what is?” asked co-convener of the Working Group Jyotsna Singh . “The woman who first approached the Court died before she could get the medicine she needed. Many more women have died while this case has continued.” Calls to invoke Patents Act safeguards to ensure treatment accessibility Activists are urging the Indian government to trigger safeguards under the Indian Patents Act, including compulsory licensing, to expand access to ribociclib and abemaciclib. They say this should be done swiftly and decisively, especially after the Central Drugs Standard Control Organization (CDSCO) submitted a counter affidavit containing contradictory information, adding a new layer of complication. At one point in the brief, the Working Group warns, CDSCO claims ribociclib is approved for the same indications as palbociclib, a generically available and thus cheaper medicine. While the two are both used in the treatment of advanced cases of cancer, ribociclib has additionally demonstrated notable benefits in early-stage cases. This means the treatment can help prevent cancer cells from returning and becoming metastatic, “when the disease is much harder to cure,” the Working Group pointed out. The formulation in CDSCO’s submission risks implying the same benefits can be expected from palbociclib. “This is not a minor discrepancy,” the Working Group insists. “It risks misleading the Court into believing that the cheaper palbociclib can replace ribociclib for early-stage breast cancer, when the data placed before the court by CDSCO itself says otherwise.” “A drug regulator has a responsibility to place clear and accurate information before the Court, particularly when women’s access to life-saving treatment is at stake,” emphasized Gargeya Telakapalli, co-coordinator of the Working Group. “The government must correct the record and act urgently to make ribociclib and abemaciclib affordable, including through compulsory licensing where monopoly pricing continues to block access.” Read more: India’s newly amended patent rules threaten affordable medicines in the Global South Renowned oncologist Dr. R. Ravi Kannan, Director of Cachar Cancer Hospital, submitted a court opinion echoing many of these observations and further clarifying the different profiles of palbociclib, ribociclib, and abemaciclib – calling for wider availability of the latter two. “Every advancement that safely reduces recurrence risk is vital,” he wrote, “because each relapse means additional financial burden on the family and risk of poverty, with the loss of cure and a return to only palliative options.” “Generic entry has historically been the single most reliable lever for expanding access to targeted cancer therapies in resource-limited settings, and there is no clinical reason to expect abemaciclib and ribociclib to be an exception,” he added. “The government cannot keep treating access to breast cancer medicines as an ordinary pricing dispute,” Singh concluded ahead of the next hearing, scheduled for September 3, 2026. “Women need the best available treatment when it can still save their lives.” People’s Health Dispatch is a fortnightly bulletin published by the People’s Health Movement and Peoples Dispatch . articles.title: “Shut Down Dilley”: Rep. Joaquin Castro on “Abusive” ICE Family Jail, Targeting of Military Families
articles.content: Calls to shut down the ICE jail known as the Dilley Immigration Processing Center in South Texas continue to grow following the detention and deportation of 5-year-old Liam Tadeo and his father Victor Martinez Nieto to Mexico. According to the family’s lawyer, Nieto had begged officers to let his son go as they were arrested on their way to soccer practice in Austin last week. Nieto wanted Liam released to his mother, but ICE reportedly refused. The arrest happened just days before Liam was set to start kindergarten. Texas Democratic Congressmember Joaquin Castro previously attempted to visit Liam and his father at Dilley but was denied by ICE . Last month, Castro led a group of more than 110 Democratic House members in a nationwide call to end family detention and shut down Dilley. “You have kids as young as 2 months old who have been in prison there,” says Castro. “And every child that’s put in there — every woman, every person — there are American investors who are making money off of their imprisonment.” Castro notes that children are not supposed to be held in detention centers for more than 20 days. “I’ve met with kids who have been there three months, seven months, 10 months. And so, this is really abusive, and it’s traumatizing a lot of kids.”

articles.title: Glacier Collapse: 2K Dead or Missing in Nepal-Tibet Flood Is “Glaring Example of Climate Injustice”
articles.content: We get a report from Nepal, where at least 547 people are confirmed to have died and over 1,500 are still missing after a glacial collapse on Wednesday sent a wall of ice, mud and rock into a Himalayan river, triggering catastrophic flooding in the Nepal-Tibet border region that swept away entire communities. Nepali authorities say they have rescued more than 3,700 people so far. Geologists say the flash floods were set off by a landslide and glacial avalanche so powerful it set off its own seismic signal. Climate scientists warn the region is warming much faster than the global average, leading to the rapid retreat of glaciers. “Scientists and civil society have been warning about the very fact that these kind of events might happen in the Himalayas,” says Sunil Acharya, a climate and public policy specialist reporting from Kathmandu, Nepal. “This is the result of the delayed global action to deal with climate change.” “The number of people being killed, the number of properties being damaged has been way beyond what we can adapt to,” says Acharya. The floods have “[washed] away hundreds of villages, a huge number of bridges and road infrastructure and also hydropower stations.”

articles.title: “Who Paid, Who Gained”: Juan González on How Chicago Funded Real Estate Instead of Social Services
articles.content: A team of researchers led by Democracy Now! ’s Juan González at the University of Illinois Chicago recently released an in-depth study on how, through a program called Tax Increment Financing ( TIF ), Chicago has spent some $16 billion in property taxes it collected over the past 40 years to fund downtown development. The money was supposed to be used to eliminate urban blight. ” TIF funding has actually exacerbated economic inequities throughout the city, pouring more than half of the billions of dollars that it collected into downtown neighborhoods while the 70 other community areas around the city were left to share the other half,” says González. Please check back later for full transcript. Page 2 Experts estimate that a language is lost every two weeks — and that half of the world’s 7,000 spoken languages could be lost by the end of the century. Quechua is the most widely spoken Indigenous language in the Americas, with approximately 7 to 10 million speakers living primarily in Peru, Bolivia and Ecuador. But like so many Indigenous languages, Qechua is vulnerable due to cultural pressures and discrimination. The new documentary Runa Simi — “our language” in Quechua — follows Fernando Valencia, a Peruvian voice actor, Indigenous activist, radio host and single father, who has dubbed many online clips of animated movies into Quechua from his home in Cusco, Peru. In the film, Fernando pursues his most ambitious goal yet: to fully dub Disney’s animated classic The Lion King into Quechua, with the help of his 8-year-old son, Dylan. “I am sharing our culture to the worldwide culture,” says Fernando Valencia, who started dubbing films after noticing that Quechua-speaking Indigenous children were watching movies dubbed into Spanish that they couldn’t understand. “There’s like one hour a week of Quechua [in school], so it is very hard to actually learn it,” says Fernando’s son Dylan, who is now 14 years old. “Indigenous people in Peru are fighting for basic rights, like having water, electricity, healthcare, education in their own language,” says Augusto Zegarra, the director of Runa Simi . “But they also have the right to access entertainment in their own language.”

articles.title: Children in Gaza are afraid flying their kites will get them killed
articles.author: Tareq S. Hajjaj
articles.content: Israel regards any kite flown in Gaza as an "act of war" and has ordered the army to treat them like drones. "I don't know what we can do that won't anger Israel," says Muhammad Owais, 13, who struggles to understand the rules of this new reality.
